tasks.short: Gather user feedback from several channels, group it by problem, analyse the sources of problems, document findings, and tell users when a problem is solved.

steps.what: User sends feedback: by e-mail or form today, through the feedback button on the site or an app review after the change
Web administrator gathers user feedback from e-mails, forms, tickets and app reviews
Web administrator groups feedback by problem in a spreadsheet

loop.input: The month's feedback items with their ticket numbers.
loop.output: Groups of feedback items per suspected problem, each listing its source items.
loop.check: The administrator checks that the items in each group really describe the same problem and that the group's name says what they describe; every group must list the ticket numbers it rests on and every item must sit in one group or in 'other'; the administrator merges or splits groups and sorts unclear items by hand.
loop.stop: One grouping per month; if rejected, the administrator groups by hand.
loop.why_not_simpler: Keyword rules miss the many ways users describe the same problem.

steps.what: Web administrator analyses user feedback to locate sources of problems
Web administrator documents findings in the knowledge base
Web administrator tells users by e-mail that their problem is solved

tasks.design: A feedback button on the site and the app review feed send feedback into the service desk ({HELPDESK}) with page and browser attached, so feedback is not gathered from several inboxes. A bounded step groups the month's feedback by suspected problem with the ticket numbers listed, and the administrator reviews each group. Findings are documented on a knowledge base template linked to the tickets. When the administrator closes a problem with a short note, users on the linked tickets are told from the service desk instead of one e-mail each. Locating the source of problems stays with the administrator.
tasks.previous_blocker: Feedback sat in several inboxes and was grouped by hand.
tasks.enabler_now: Service desks gather feedback; language models group free text with traceable sources.
tasks.still_hard: Vague feedback cannot be grouped well.
tasks.human_edge: Seeing that two different complaints have one cause.
tasks.altitude: The administrator reviews groups instead of sorting feedback.

reach.learn: Whether they hear back when it is fixed.

evidence.claim: TOPdesk suggests ticket category and priority, summarises tickets and drafts knowledge items for review.
Feedback with contact details is personal data and is kept only as long as needed.

assumptions: Boundary: from user feedback to users told; fixing problems is outside.
Input contract: feedback button and review feed linked to the service desk; fallback is the inboxes.
Users' time does not change; their feedback is shown in s6. s4 keeps 80: the template links the tickets, but the findings are the administrator's own writing.
s5 is part of informing users of problem resolutions, which sibling task 15-1299.01:14752 covers; its saving is counted there, so s5 keeps its full time here.
research_questions: How often does the administrator change a group?

already_counted.description: Web administrator reviews, merges and splits proposed groups.

incremental.description: Web administrator keeps the feedback channels linked.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: little feedback comes through the button, so the inboxes stay and s1 keeps 70, and proposed groups need much rework, so s2 keeps 80 (14.8); high: a busy site with feedback through the service desk as designed (29.7).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Decide what to monitor, configure monitoring checks, test alerts, document the setup, and tune noisy alerts.

steps.what: Web administrator decides what to monitor and sets thresholds
Web administrator sets up monitoring tools on web servers and sites through the tool's screens
Web administrator tests that alerts fire and reach the right people
Web administrator documents the monitoring setup
Web administrator maintains monitoring by tuning noisy alerts from the alert history

tasks.design: Monitoring checks are kept as code in the repository with templates per site type ({OTHER}), so new sites get checks by copying a template instead of clicking through the tool's screens. The pipeline runs a test alert for each new check, and the setup page is generated from the check definitions. An alert history report lists the noisiest alerts, so tuning starts there. Deciding what to monitor and the thresholds stays with the administrator.
tasks.previous_blocker: Checks were set up by hand per site and documented separately.
tasks.enabler_now: Monitoring tools accept checks as code and report alert history.
tasks.still_hard: Older servers need agents installed by hand.
tasks.human_edge: Knowing which alert really means customers are affected.

reach.learn: Whether alerts are fewer and clearer.

evidence.claim: Monitoring tools can take check definitions as code and generate documentation from them.
Organisations under the national cyber security law must take measures to keep systems available.

assumptions: Boundary: from the site in service to alerts tuned; responding to incidents is outside.
Input contract: monitoring tool supports checks as code; fallback is setup through screens.
Threshold decisions stay with the administrator.
On-call colleagues' time does not change.

incremental.description: Web administrator keeps check templates current.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: many older servers are still set up through the screens, so s2 keeps 80 and their setup is documented by hand, so s4 keeps 70 (21.5); high: standard sites from templates as designed (35.0).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Read newsletters, blogs and release notes, attend conferences and meetups, take online courses, and share notes with the team.

steps.what: Web administrator monitors web developments by reading newsletters, blogs and release notes
Web administrator participates in professional conferences, workshops and meetups
Web administrator takes online courses
Web administrator shares notes with the team: by e-mail today, on a team wiki page per topic after the change

tasks.design: A feed reader gathers chosen newsletters, blogs and the release notes of the tools the team runs ({OTHER}), so the administrator reads one list instead of many inboxes and sites, and release notes for tools in use are marked. Notes go on a team wiki page per topic ({DOCS}) instead of e-mails; writing them keeps its time. Attending events and courses stays with the administrator.
tasks.previous_blocker: Sources were spread over inboxes and sites and notes sent as e-mails.
tasks.enabler_now: Feed readers gather sources and mark release notes.
tasks.still_hard: Much useful knowledge is shared only at events.
tasks.human_edge: Judging which new technique is worth trying here.

evidence.claim: Feed readers can gather newsletters, blogs and release notes in one list.

assumptions: Boundary: from new developments to notes shared; applying them is outside.
Input contract: sources chosen by the administrator; fallback is inboxes.
Events, courses and writing notes do not change. s1 keeps 80: reading stays; opening many inboxes and sites drops.

incremental.description: Web administrator prunes the source list.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: the feed misses many sources, so the administrator still checks inboxes and sites and s1 keeps 90 (3.5); high: chosen sources in one feed as designed (7.5).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Collect existing rules and examples, decide guidelines with the content team, write the style guide, check it, and publish it.

steps.what: Editors add rules and example pages to the shared folder as they come across them
Web administrator collects existing rules, examples and brand guidance
Web administrator develops style guidelines with the content team
Web administrator documents the style guidelines with examples

loop.input: The list of decided rules and the collected good and bad examples.
loop.output: Draft guide sections with a rule, a reason and an example each.
loop.check: The administrator checks that each section states the rule as it was decided and that each example really follows the rule it illustrates; every rule in the draft must match one on the decided list, or it is dropped; examples are taken only from the collected material; the administrator edits every section.
loop.stop: One draft per section; if rejected, the administrator writes it.
loop.why_not_simpler: A template gives the layout, not the wording of each rule and its example.

steps.what: Web administrator checks the final style guide
Web administrator publishes the checked guide as a new version on the intranet, which notifies editors: by e-mail today

tasks.design: Existing rules, brand guidance and example pages are gathered in one shared folder ({DOCS}) that editors add to, so the administrator does not search for them. A bounded step drafts guide sections from the decided rules and the collected examples; rules not on the decided list are dropped and the administrator edits every section. Once checked, the administrator publishes the guide as a new version on the intranet ({CMS}), which notifies editors. Deciding the rules stays with the administrator and content team.
tasks.previous_blocker: Rules were scattered and the guide written from scratch.
tasks.enabler_now: Language models draft sections that can be checked against a list of decided rules.
tasks.still_hard: Editors follow examples more than rules.
tasks.human_edge: Choosing rules that editors will actually follow.
tasks.altitude: The administrator edits the guide instead of writing it from scratch.

evidence.claim: Language models can draft guide sections that can be checked against a list of decided rules.

assumptions: Boundary: from the guide needed to the guide published; enforcing the guide is outside.
Input contract: editors add examples to the shared folder; fallback is searching.
The administrator checks the guide before publishing.
Editors add examples to the shared folder (s6, share 1). s3 keeps 75: sections are drafted from the decided rules, but the administrator still writes and edits the guide.
research_questions: How much of each drafted section is kept?

already_counted.description: Web administrator edits drafted guide sections.

incremental.description: Web administrator keeps the examples folder tidy.

approvals.approved_version: The style guide exactly as checked by the administrator in s4, published once as the new version on the intranet guide page; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: a new guide with many decisions and few examples in the folder, so s1 keeps 80 and s3 keeps 90 (16.4); high: an update of an existing guide as designed (26.3).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The web administrator keeps locating problems, deciding monitoring and guidelines and learning; gathered feedback, hand-set checks, scattered reading and written-from-scratch guides shrink.
role.ambitious_version: An administrator with more time on the site's quality.
